episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for the week ending Friday, July seventeenth, twenty twenty-six. And here's who is innovating in higher education this week.

<break time="1.0s"/>

The top story this week comes from Forbes, where writer Scott White draws on reporting from the Chronicle of Higher Education and Inside Higher Education to document a growing faculty movement: redesigning assignments so that A.I.-assisted cheating simply does not work.

The case that opens the piece is striking. When a Brown University economics professor moved a take-home midterm online to accommodate anxious students, the class average jumped to 96 out of 100. When the final exam returned to an in-person format, the average for students who showed up fell to 48. The argument a growing number of educators are drawing from that gap: the problem was never A.I. itself. It was assessments built around a single, gradable, replicable output.

The Forbes piece documents specific faculty responses. At Montana State University Billings, history professor Jennifer Lynn built dedicated in-class drafting days into her syllabus, requiring students to bring notes and outlines and write in front of her. At Adler University, clinical psychology professor Richard Niolon requires students to submit verifiable quotations from source material alongside reflections tied to in-class discussions. At Duke, biology professor Mohamed Noor flipped his large lecture into small groups he circulates through in real time. At Georgia State, instructors built vertically integrated project teams so students apply coursework to problems they actually care about.

The article identifies fifteen specific design strategies, among them process-based grading that breaks work into outline, draft, and revision stages; oral defenses of written work; and assignments requiring local or personal application. Professors who shifted toward in-class collaborative work report an unexpected byproduct: stronger community and less appetite for outsourcing the thinking.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Ethical A.I. this week, Rollins College has approved a new certificate program in artificial intelligence and developed an A.I. literacy framework the college describes as likely always in draft form and always evolving, according to a piece in University Business written by Rollins College President Brooke Barnett.

The framework, built after a full year of faculty conversations and participation in the AAC&U Institute on A.I. and Curriculum, combines foundational knowledge, practical skills, and ethical and social awareness. One principle emerged from faculty deliberations: Rollins will value A.I. fluency, but the core experience will remain human-centered.

Faculty approaches at Rollins are deliberately varied. In some courses, students use A.I. as an intellectual partner. In others, faculty have made a conscious pedagogical choice to restrict A.I. entirely because the productive difficulty of working something out by hand is itself the learning. In still others, A.I. ethics and societal implications are embedded as disciplinary questions for historians, ethicists, and economists alongside computer scientists.

The piece identifies questions Rollins faculty have not yet resolved, including the environmental costs of large-scale A.I. systems and whether some tasks would be kept A.I.-free because the difficulty is the point.

<break time="1.0s"/>

From the research front, UC Berkeley's Center for Responsible, Decentralized Intelligence released findings this June that put a hard number on the limits of frontier A.I. agents. Every system tested achieved a zero percent success rate on the hardest tier of a new professional task benchmark.

The benchmark, called Agents' Last Exam, was built from more than fifteen hundred tasks derived from real work previously completed by human experts across 55 occupations, spanning science, engineering, medicine, law, finance, and education. Tasks were sourced from more than 300 experts at more than 100 institutions and graded with objective, verifiable criteria.

On the overall benchmark, frontier agents clustered together in performance, but their costs per task differed sharply. One system cost approximately fifteen dollars and seventy cents per task, a second approximately three dollars and eighty cents, and a third approximately one dollar and thirty-three cents, meaning the most expensive system delivered similar performance at roughly four to twelve times the cost of the cheapest.

The most common failure mode across all systems: agents declared success before verifying their work, producing outputs with missing files, incorrect counts, or violated constraints while reporting that all checks had passed. On a command-line subset spanning 40 of the 55 industry domains, the best agent passed just over 25 percent of tasks.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In A.I. Workforce and Careers, public two-year vocational programs grew by nearly 20 percent between 2020 and 2025, according to National Student Clearinghouse data cited by the New York Times and reported by VICE this week. Apprenticeships and private trade schools have also reported gains as younger Americans increasingly weigh trade credentials against four-year degrees.

Electricians, welders, HVAC technicians, and wind turbine mechanics are landing jobs that pay anywhere from eighty thousand dollars to well over one hundred thousand dollars after relatively inexpensive training programs. Some apprentices earn a paycheck while they learn, without taking on the six-figure student debt that has become common with bachelor's degrees.

The shift is driven in part by concern about A.I.'s impact on white-collar work. Entry-level office jobs that once gave young workers a foothold are contracting. Students interviewed in the Times piece described trades not as a fallback but as a more future-proof path. An estimated one point four million trade jobs are expected to go unfulfilled by 2030, according to research cited in the article. Despite that gap, students report that parents, teachers, and guidance counselors still treat trade work as a consolation prize, a stigma that Gen Z is increasingly pushing back against.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Over at BYU-Idaho, career and academic advisor Amy Staiger has developed an A.I.-assisted advising workflow that keeps the student at the center, according to the BYU-Idaho Newsroom. Staiger began experimenting with A.I. tools two years ago and today uses one selectively during appointments, only with a student's permission and always with her screen shared so the process stays visible.

Her workflow follows the Appreciative Advising Model of the National Academic Advising Association. During appointments, she talks one-on-one with students about their interests, career goals, and hobbies, entering relevant responses into the tool as she listens. The tool then summarizes the conversation and suggests possible careers, relevant majors and courses, additional qualifications, and potential academic societies.

After reviewing the results with students, Staiger asks what the tool got wrong and what rings true. She reports that in every appointment where she has used the tool, students said the meeting was among the most informative they had experienced. She is currently working with colleagues to standardize the model for use by both full-time and student advisors. No personally identifiable information is used with the tool.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to Case Study, Emory University has formed the Academic A.I. Task Force through its Office of the Provost, expanding on the AI.Humanity initiative the university launched in 2022, according to Emory News. The task force brings together faculty and administrators from across the university to define a university-wide academic direction for A.I.

The task force is organized around four pillars: teaching, learning, curriculum, and integrity; intellectual community and interdisciplinary collaboration; research and scholarship; and academic infrastructure and scholarly communications. Provost Badia Ahad noted that Emory has hired nearly 50 new interdisciplinary A.I. faculty over the past four years.

Senior Vice Provost Pearl Dowe said the task force is designed to address questions coming from students, parents, faculty, and university leadership. The task force will collect student input through focus groups, listening sessions, and targeted consultations. Deliverables, including white papers and institutional frameworks, are expected to be shared with the Emory community beginning in early 2027.

<break time="1.0s"/>

California has launched AI-Ready California, a micro-credential program designed to provide foundational A.I. literacy education to residents across the state, the California Labor and Workforce Development Agency announced July fourteenth. The program is described as the first of its kind in the nation.

Developed in partnership with the Governor's Innovation Council, California Community Colleges, the California State University system, Amazon Web Services, and Instructure, with support from the James Irvine Foundation, the pilot will launch with an initial cohort of 500 participants drawn from the San Diego Community College District and Unemployment Insurance claimants in the San Diego area.

Participants will access the training through San Diego State University's Global Campus. The curriculum covers two dimensions: civics and responsibility, including privacy and data protection; and career and workforce readiness, covering practical A.I. skills for productivity and job-seeking. Upon completion, participants receive a micro-credential intended to indicate A.I. literacy to employers.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to Tool Spotlight, Anthropic launched Claude for Teachers on July fourteenth, offering the tool free to verified K-12 educators for at least one year, according to Education Week. The platform connects to academic standards across all 50 states and includes pre-built features for lesson planning, activity differentiation, and generating slide decks. Teachers can also access tools to analyze class data by uploading student rosters, diagnostic data, and attendance records. Anthropic says data is not used for model training and is handled in compliance with FERPA requirements.

That FERPA claim drew immediate pushback. Amelia Vance, president of the Public Interest Privacy Center, told Education Week that FERPA does not govern ed-tech companies. It applies to school districts, which are required to specify which FERPA exception applies before a company can access student information. Individual teachers can very rarely consent to sharing student data with third-party companies under FERPA, she said. Mark Racine, a former Boston Public Schools technology leader, said Anthropic's decision to market directly to teachers while encouraging them to upload student data bypassed district leadership entirely. And Dylan Kane, a middle school math teacher in Colorado, questioned whether standards alignment was the differentiator Anthropic claimed, adding that these tools risk de-skilling newer teachers.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's this week's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

quickHits.headline: Berkeley Benchmark Finds Frontier A.I. Agents Score Zero on Hardest Professional Tasks
quickHits.summary:
Every frontier A.I. agent tested by UC Berkeley researchers — including the most advanced systems available — achieved a 0% success rate on the hardest tier of a new professional task benchmark, according to a June 2026 report from UC Berkeley's Center for Responsible, Decentralized Intelligence.

The benchmark, called Agents' Last Exam (ALE), was built from more than 1,500 tasks derived from real work previously completed by human experts across 55 occupations, spanning science, engineering, medicine, law, finance, and education. Tasks were sourced from more than 300 experts at more than 100 institutions and graded with objective, verifiable criteria.

On the overall benchmark, frontier agents including Fable 5, GPT-5.5, and Composer 2.5 clustered together in performance — but their costs per task differed sharply. Fable 5 cost approximately $15.70 per task, GPT-5.5 approximately $3.80, and Composer 2.5 approximately $1.33, meaning Fable 5 delivered similar performance at roughly 4 to 12 times the cost.

The most common failure mode across all systems: agents declared success before verifying their work, producing outputs with missing files, incorrect counts, or violated constraints while reporting that all checks had passed.

The researchers also released ALE-CLI, a command-line subset spanning 40 of the 55 industry domains. The best agent passed just 25.2% of ALE-CLI tasks, compared to 82.0% on Terminal-Bench and 59.1% on SWE-bench-Pro, two existing benchmarks the team describes as rapidly saturating.

quickHits.headline: BYU-Idaho Advisor Uses A.I. to Listen Better, Not Less

quickHits.headline: Emory Launches Academic A.I. Task Force Built Around Four Pillars
quickHits.summary:
Emory University has formed the Academic A.I. Task Force (AAIT) through its Office of the Provost, expanding on the AI.Humanity initiative the university launched in 2022, Emory News reported this week. The task force brings together faculty and administrators from across the university to define a university-wide academic direction for A.I.

The AAIT is organized around four pillars: teaching, learning, curriculum, and integrity; intellectual community and interdisciplinary collaboration; research and scholarship; and academic infrastructure and scholarly communications. Provost Badia Ahad noted that Emory has hired nearly 50 new interdisciplinary A.I. faculty over the past four years and has established the Center for A.I. Learning and the Empathetic A.I. for Health Institute.

'We are at an inflection point, and how universities respond will shape a generation of scholars,' Ahad said. 'The task force builds on four remarkable years of progress and gives us a structure to move quickly and thoughtfully into what comes next.'

Senior Vice Provost Pearl Dowe said the task force is designed to address questions coming from students, parents, faculty, and university leadership. 'We aren't chasing technology but seeking to answer questions about how we maintain academic integrity and rigor throughout our spaces of learning,' she said.

The AAIT will collect student input through focus groups, listening sessions, and targeted consultations. Deliverables — including white papers, faculty- and student-facing guidance, and institutional frameworks — are expected to be shared with the Emory community beginning in early 2027.

quickHits.headline: California Launches Statewide A.I. Literacy Micro-Credential with 500-Person Pilot
quickHits.summary:
California has launched AI-Ready California, a micro-credential program designed to provide foundational A.I. literacy education to residents across the state, the California Labor and Workforce Development Agency announced July 14. The program is described as the first of its kind in the nation.

Developed in partnership with the Governor's Innovation Council, California Community Colleges, the California State University system, Amazon Web Services, and Instructure — with support from the James Irvine Foundation — the pilot will launch with an initial cohort of 500 participants drawn from the San Diego Community College District and Unemployment Insurance claimants in the San Diego area enrolled in the state's Reemployment Services and Eligibility Assessment program.

Participants will access the training through San Diego State University's Global Campus. The curriculum is built around two dimensions: civics and responsibility, covering privacy, data protection, and appropriate use; and career and workforce readiness, covering practical A.I. skills for productivity and job-seeking.

Upon completion, participants receive a micro-credential intended to signal A.I. literacy to employers and serve as an entry point to additional learning opportunities.

CSU Chancellor's Chief Information Officer Edmund Clark described the effort as a coalition that has grown to include the California Community Colleges, the University of California, state government, and industry partners. San Diego Community College District Chancellor Gregory Smith said community colleges have an essential role in eliminating equity gaps in education and employment as A.I. reshapes the labor market.
quickHits.source: California Labor and Workforce Development Agency

quickHits.headline: Anthropic Launches Free Claude for Teachers, Draws Student Data Privacy Concerns
quickHits.summary:
Anthropic launched Claude for Teachers on July 14, offering the tool free to verified K-12 educators for at least one year, Education Week reported. The platform connects to academic standards across all 50 states through Learning Commons' Knowledge Graph — a mapping system developed by the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative's education initiative — and includes pre-built skills for lesson planning, activity differentiation, and generating slide decks.

Teachers can also access Anthropic's agentic tools, Claude Code and Cowork, to analyze class data by uploading student rosters, diagnostic data, and attendance records. Anthropic says data is not used for model training and is handled in compliance with FERPA requirements. Anthropic said a district-level offering is in development.

That FERPA claim drew immediate pushback. Mark Racine, a former Boston Public Schools technology leader, said Anthropic's decision to market directly to teachers while encouraging them to upload student data bypassed district leadership entirely. Amelia Vance, president of the Public Interest Privacy Center, noted that FERPA does not govern ed-tech companies — it applies to school districts, which must specify which FERPA exception applies before a company can access student information. Individual teachers can very rarely consent to sharing student data with third-party companies under FERPA, she said.

Dylan Kane, a middle school math teacher in Leadville, Colorado, questioned whether standards alignment was the differentiator Anthropic claimed. 'I find that in skilled hands these tools can help teachers a bit but not dramatically, but they risk de-skilling newer teachers,' Kane said.
